one_liner: Ahead-of-time TypeScript-to-native compiler; executables start in about 2 ms against tens of milliseconds for Node and Bun, but run hot loops slower.
what_it_does: scriptc compiles a typed subset of TypeScript/JavaScript, plus a large slice of the Node.js 24 API (fs, http/https, net, tls, crypto, child_process, zlib, fetch), into a standalone native executable, a static library (--lib) or a WASI Preview 1 module. You keep your .ts sources and run `scriptc build app.ts -o app` instead of `node app.ts`. A static build contains no JavaScript engine. `--dynamic` embeds quickjs-ng for npm dependencies and `any`-typed code. `scriptc coverage` reports which statements compile statically, which need the engine and which are unsupported.
how_it_is_fast: The TypeScript checker's types and narrowing drive lowering to a typed IR: generics are specialized, unions become tagged values and closures get explicit captures. LLVM 22 then compiles that IR at -O2 and links it against a precompiled C runtime pack. Startup does no engine initialization, parsing, bytecode compilation or JIT warm-up, so process start costs little more than exec plus the C runtime's init. Memory is managed by reference counting with a cycle collector run at defined collection points, not a garbage-collected engine heap, which keeps idle RSS in the low MiB.
when_to_use: Short-lived CLIs, git hooks, editor helpers or build steps that run many times, where Node's 20-60 ms process start dominates wall time.
Small node:http services or sidecars where idle RSS matters (launch coverage reports 1.9 MiB idle; an HN commenter measured 2.5 MiB vs 181 MiB for Node).
Shipping a single-file binary to machines without Node: static builds need no runtime, and npm dependencies are embedded at build time with --dynamic.
Embedding TypeScript logic in C/C++, iOS (arm64) or Android (API 26+) apps as a library-mode static archive, or in a browser or WASI host as a Wasm reactor.
Strictly typed codebases where `scriptc coverage` reports 100% static, with little `any` and few npm dependencies.
when_not_to_use: Throughput-bound hot loops. V8's JIT still wins: issue #357 measured xorshift32 77.4x slower than Node 24.12.0 before the fix and at parity after it, but a byte loop stayed 2.75x slower (3.22 vs 1.17 ms/round, derived from page data). Issue #113 (scriptc 0.0.23) reported byte loops 2.1x to 6.5x slower than Node 22, and one HN commenter reported about 7.5x slower on byte arrays.

Code dominated by npm packages or `any`. That code runs in the embedded quickjs-ng interpreter, and values copied across the boundary are validated at runtime. Snippets of launch coverage report Hono under --dynamic at 18.4k requests/s vs 70.5k for Bun.

Programs that need N-API/.node addons, worker_threads Worker, Float16 or BigInt64 typed arrays, resizable or transferable ArrayBuffers, Date setters or locale formatting, object-to-primitive `==`, or other features listed as unsupported on the limitations page.
Network servers on Windows or WASI. The Windows loop polls sockets with zero-timeout WSAPoll and a capped (~1 ms) nanosleep instead of IOCP; the source comments say it is sized for dozens of sockets.
Production code that needs exact Node semantics or a stable toolchain. The project is a self-described Vercel Labs experiment at 0.2.x, and 0.2.0 removed the C backend and the --emit=c output.

integration.form: compiler CLI (npm package `scriptc` with a native platform binary, or a standalone archive from GitHub Releases) that emits native executables, library-mode static archives, object/LLVM/IR files or WASI modules
integration.dependencies: a platform linker and SDK/sysroot for executables (Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS) and Zig for cross-linking to Linux, Windows and WASI. The compiler bundles the TypeScript 7 native checker and the LLVM 22 helper. The runtime vendors mbedTLS, curl, zlib, ryu and Unicode tables, plus quickjs-ng (linked only with --dynamic)
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js 24+ and npm for installation (not needed to compile or run). GNU/Linux compiler and runtime packs need glibc 2.34+. The LLVM helper needs macOS 15+ (artifacts target macOS 14). iOS 15.0 and Android API 26 minimums for library mode.
integration.platforms: macOS arm64/x64, Linux x64/arm64 (glibc or musl), Windows x64; iOS arm64 and Android arm64 in library mode only; WASI Preview 1 (no sockets, child processes or signals)
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded script runtime with non-atomic reference counts and a fiber-based event loop (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, WSAPoll on Windows). worker_threads Worker is unsupported; child_process.fork re-executes the binary. FFI callbacks from foreign threads are queued to the event loop. Library mode can make runtime state per-thread with abi.instance_per_thread.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the same TypeScript source and many Node 24 APIs compile, but only the typed subset runs natively. `any` code and npm code need --dynamic (quickjs-ng), addons are unsupported, and runtime behavior differs from Node in documented ways.

gotchas: Statically typed out-of-bounds reads from typed arrays abort the process, where Node returns undefined. Runtime traps cannot be caught; only thrown values and supported exceptions can.

Strings are stored as UTF-8 but indexed with JavaScript's UTF-16 semantics. On non-ASCII strings, slice, charCodeAt, indexOf and similar calls must map UTF-16 positions to byte offsets. Issue #261 measured slice on a 20 MB string at 21 ms before the fix. The current runtime keeps checkpoints every 4 KiB for strings of 64 KiB or more, but only in four sparse cache entries per runtime, so indexing more than four large non-ASCII strings in turn can fall back to prefix scans.

Semantics differ quietly from Node. Object.keys and JSON.stringify follow declaration order, not insertion order. `JSON.parse(s) as T` validates at runtime and throws. A record converted to a narrower shape is copied, so mutations through it do not reach the original. Uncaught exceptions print `Uncaught <value>` with no stack trace. Cycles through native handles, or across the static/quickjs-ng boundary, can leak.

Harness and provenance flaw behind the headline: the 1.78 ms vs 21.29 ms (Bun 1.3.12) vs 61.78 ms (Node 24.18.0) startup figures exist only in news-article search snippets about scriptc 0.0.16 (current release 0.2.4), with no named runner, program or hardware. Their Node figure is 3.3x the 18.6 ms an HN commenter measured for Node 24, which points to a heavier program or slower machine, so treat the 12x and 35x ratios as order-of-magnitude only. No benchmark in the repo compares against Node or Bun; benchmarks/builds measures compile latency.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick scriptc over LLRT when your code is typed TypeScript and you want compiled native code and a single binary rather than a QuickJS interpreter with no JIT. Pick it over Porffor or katsu when you need a working Node API surface (http/https, tls, fs, child_process, fetch) as well as fast startup. For untyped JavaScript or compute-heavy work, stay on Node or Bun.
verified_claims_summary: Snippets of launch news coverage (InfoQ and others, all blocked here) report median CLI startup for scriptc 0.0.16 executables of 1.78 ms, against 21.29 ms for Bun 1.3.12 and 61.78 ms for Node 24.18.0, and 1.9 MiB idle memory for a framework-free node:http server. Runner, hardware and program are not stated, and no repo benchmark reproduces the run. On sustained throughput scriptc loses: issue #357 (Ryzen 9 7900X, Linux, scriptc 0.1.3 LLVM release build, clang 22.1.8, Node 24.12.0) reached parity on xorshift32 only after a fix, and its byte loop stayed about 2.75x slower than Node.
status_note: Very active: last commit 2026-10-06, 939 commits, release 0.2.4, Apache-2.0. It is labelled a Vercel Labs experiment, so it is usable for typed CLIs and small servers today, but flags and semantics still change between 0.x releases.
